definition: A set of reinforcing loops in which each turn makes the next one easier, so momentum builds over time. In this repo NVIDIA's flywheel has four loops (developer, scale/R&D, full-stack, capital) that share one hub: revenue and gross profit.
The number of a vendor's products already in use. A large installed base of CUDA-capable GPUs (over 1 billion by 2020, per NVIDIA) makes CUDA the default target for developers and researchers.
When revenue grows faster than costs, so each extra dollar of sales adds more than a dollar's share of profit. NVIDIA's R&D rose 14× from FY2016 to FY2026 yet fell from 27% to about 9% of revenue.

Binding commitments to buy inventory, components or manufacturing capacity in the future, disclosed in a company's filings. NVIDIA's supply and capacity commitments reached $279B in Q2 FY2027; they secure scarce supply but must be paid even if demand falls.
The fraction of a customer's total spending in a category that goes to one vendor. Selling racks, networking, CPUs and software rather than only GPUs raises NVIDIA's share of each data-center dollar.

NVIDIA's 2025 program that licenses NVLink so partners' custom CPUs and accelerators can join an NVLink scale-up domain alongside NVIDIA GPUs. Announced partners include Qualcomm, Fujitsu, MediaTek, Marvell and AWS (Trainium4).
A cloud provider specialised in renting GPU capacity for AI (for example CoreWeave, Lambda, Nebius, Crusoe), as opposed to a general-purpose hyperscaler. Several are NVIDIA investees or partners.

The critique that a supplier inflates its own demand by investing in, lending to or guaranteeing capacity for customers who then use the money to buy the supplier's products. Applied to NVIDIA's stakes in AI labs and neoclouds and its capacity backstops.

A deal that hires a target company's team, usually with a technology licence, instead of buying the company outright. It is faster than an acquisition and can avoid merger review; NVIDIA's Groq and Enfabrica deals used this structure.
